items.stimulus: A city planning office in Larkspur selected a random sample of 300 residents from a list of all Larkspur residents who commute to work by bicycle. Of the residents surveyed, 246 said they favor adding a protected bike lane to Main Avenue.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Most Larkspur residents favor adding a protected bike lane to Main Avenue.
Most Larkspur residents who commute by car oppose adding a protected bike lane to Main Avenue.
Most Larkspur residents who commute by bicycle favor adding a protected bike lane to Main Avenue.
Exactly 82% of Larkspur bicycle commuters favor adding a protected bike lane to Main Avenue.
items.explanation: The sample was drawn at random from Larkspur residents who commute by bicycle, so the result applies to that group only. In the sample, 246 out of 300 (82%) favor the bike lane, which is a large majority. So you can conclude that most Larkspur bicycle commuters favor it.

B.why: You assumed that car commuters would react the opposite way from bicycle commuters. No car commuters were surveyed, so the data say nothing about them.

D.why: You treated the sample percentage as the exact population value. A different random sample would probably give a slightly different percentage, so 82% is only an estimate.

items.stimulus: A paleobotany team kept a list of every volunteer who had worked at least one full season at Ridgeback Quarry, a fossil-leaf dig site. The team chose 200 people from this list at random and asked whether they would rather split shale by hand or use a power saw. Of the 200 people, 168 chose splitting by hand and 32 chose the power saw.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Most volunteers at fossil dig sites in general would rather split shale by hand than use a power saw.
Most people who have never volunteered at Ridgeback Quarry would rather use a power saw than split shale by hand.
Most volunteers who have worked a season at Ridgeback Quarry would rather split shale by hand than use a power saw.
Among all Ridgeback Quarry volunteers, exactly 136 more prefer splitting shale by hand than prefer using a power saw.
items.explanation: The sample was drawn at random from one group: volunteers who have worked at least one season at Ridgeback Quarry. In the sample, 168 of 200 people (84%) preferred splitting by hand, which is far more than the 32 who chose the saw. You can therefore conclude that most people in that same group prefer splitting by hand. The word 'most' keeps the claim to what a sample can support.

A.why: You stretched the result to volunteers at every fossil dig site. Only Ridgeback Quarry volunteers could have been chosen, so the survey says nothing about volunteers anywhere else.

B.why: You assumed people outside the sampled group would answer the opposite way. Nobody who had never volunteered at Ridgeback Quarry was surveyed, so the data never tested that group.

D.why: 168 − 32 = 136 is the gap inside the sample of 200. It is not an exact count for the whole list of volunteers. A random sample gives you an estimate, not an exact figure.

items.stimulus: A marine park issues a night-dive certification to divers who complete its nighttime reef training. A marine biologist chose 120 divers at random from everyone holding this certification and asked whether the park should extend night-dive hours to protect feeding octopuses less. Of the 120 divers, 96 were in favor of extending the hours and 24 were opposed.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Most divers who hold the park's night-dive certification are in favor of extending the night-dive hours.
Most divers at the park who lack the night-dive certification are opposed to extending the night-dive hours.
Most visitors to the marine park, whether or not they dive, are in favor of extending the night-dive hours.
Among certified night divers, the percent in favor exceeds the percent opposed by 72 percentage points.
items.explanation: The sample was drawn at random from divers who hold the park's night-dive certification. In the sample, 96 of 120 (80%) were in favor and only 24 (20%) were opposed. So you can conclude that most certified night divers are in favor. That claim is about the same group that was sampled, and it uses 'most' instead of an exact figure.

B.why: You reversed the condition that defined the group and assumed uncertified divers would vote the other way. No uncertified divers were surveyed, so the data can't tell you what they think.

C.why: You widened the result to every visitor to the park. The sample came only from certified night divers, so it can't be used to generalize to all visitors.

D.why: 72 is the gap in head counts (96 − 24), not the gap in percents. The sample percents are 80% and 20%, which differ by 60 percentage points. You treated a count difference as a percent difference.

items.stimulus: A weavers' guild keeps a separate roster of its members who dye their yarn using only natural dyes, such as madder root and indigo. A textile historian chose 80 people at random from this roster and asked how each had first learned to weave. Of the 80 people, 64 said they learned from a family member and 16 said they learned in a class.
items.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Most hand-loom weavers across the country first learned to weave from a member of their own family.
Most of the guild's members who use synthetic dyes first learned to weave by taking a class.
Among the guild's natural-dye weavers, about three times as many learned from family as learned in a class.
Most of the guild's natural-dye weavers first learned to weave from a member of their own family.
items.explanation: The sample was drawn at random from one group: guild members who use only natural dyes. In the sample, 64 of 80 (80%) learned from a family member, far more than the 16 who learned in a class. So you can conclude that most of the guild's natural-dye weavers learned from family. That conclusion stays within the sampled group and uses 'most' instead of an exact number.

A.why: You extended the result to all hand-loom weavers in the country. Only natural-dye members of a single guild could have been chosen, so the result can't be generalized that far.

B.why: You switched to the opposite group, the synthetic-dye weavers, and assumed they would answer the other way. None of them were surveyed, so the data can't support any claim about them.

C.why: You divided the gap by the smaller count: (64 − 16) ÷ 16 = 3. The ratio is actually 64 ÷ 16 = 4. That means about four times as many, not three, so this comparison is wrong.
